text:
Two talks from Granola's design engineering night that I'm thinking about 👇
 
1. Maggie Appleton (GitHubMaggie Appleton (GitHub Next) on speculative design.
I've been following Maggie's work since her writing on digital gardens, where ideas grow wiki-style instead of being published as finished posts in chronological order.

She talked about her work at the R&D labs of GitHub, noticing weak signals, asking what might happen next, then building a prototype that lets people actually examine that future. At ∗codeplain we're asking the same question about software development: what are the signals and how will we develop software in Sept 2027?

2. Vlad Moroz (Paper) on the shape of color.
I never took too much time thinking about how color pickers in design tools are made, but they affect every designer's work. How do you preserve readability and perceived intensity when changing hues?

Vlad showed how the same HSL lightness can have very different perceived brightness across hues. Paper maps each OKLCH hue slice into a rectangular picker so colors stay in gamut and hue shifts feel consistent. And agents still default to hex, so I keep wondering what they'd design like if they thought in OKLCH.

Thanks Granola for opening your office and hosting the 10th edition of the design eng night!

text:
1.5 days. That's how long it took from my first Figma screen to Forgettable running on my iPhone.
Forgettable is for the thought that ruins my mornings: did I lock the door? Is the oven off? Did I switch off the lights?
You can't check from the office, so the doubt follows you all day.
I started from one belief. A reminder only works if it comes by itself. If you have to remember to open a reminder app, you've already forgotten.
So the app reacts to what happens around you:
→ you leave or arrive somewhere (a 150 m circle the phone watches, even with the app closed)
→ you drop off or join your home Wi-Fi
→ a set time, or a real alarm that cuts through silent mode
At home it's never just you, so the list can be shared. "Anna locked the door at 08:12" means nobody has to ask anymore.
I designed every screen in Figma and built it with Claude Code. iOS and Android, widgets, Siri, shared households, plus a website with help guides and a privacy policy.
Setting it up takes under a minute: pick the usual suspects (front door, stove, windows), set your home once, done.
The name comes from Neville's Remembrall in Harry Potter. It turned red when he forgot something, but never told him what. This one does.
What's the one thing you always go back to check?
P.S. Swipe through the slides for the screens. Link to the website is in the first comment.

text: If you are building skills for the developer community, please budget very experienced team member time to build evals and garden the set of skills. As models continue to improve, it is beneficial to user outcomes and token efficiency to prune either portions or entire skills that the base model and harness are freshly capable of doing better. This is similar to long-established good habits of tending our code bases as languages, libraries, and SDKs advance.

Much like we did with @aisdk, we're bringing a truly open-source, runtime-agnostic solution to harness durability.

We're extending the durability infra that powers @eve and Workflows to all harnesses, like Pi and OpenCode. Local, Vercel, or DIY.

Fun fact: even Claude Code and Codex can be made durable (and observable!) this way. The catch: they're not (currently) designed for embedding, which makes them less efficient, less portable, and brings an extra sandbox requirement compared to Pi or Fx.

What used to take weeks in C++ now takes one hour or so in Rust with a half-burned ChatGPT Pro plan and much less code. Plus a real-time viz for fun. Most of what I did was to review and agree on some architecture SVGs with the agent before letting it loose.

The idea is that a performant single-threaded high-bandwidth data recorder owns buffer lifecycles for reuse and performs memory-to-storage DMAs via io_uring as much as possible. While also planning to allow DMAs from "foreign-owned" pinned memory like mmap() and CUDA with ref counting for ownership release.

Adding open-source dependencies in Rust really feels like a breeze thanks to the well-maintained crate registry.

text:
🤗 transformers serve now speaks 🔊

We just added an OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/speech` endpoint to transformers serve, and we couldn't have picked a better model to launch it with than Phonon, Gradium brand-new on-device TTS: tiny, fast and multilingual.

Test it with:
transformers serve gradium/phonon-40m-en

Phonon isn't alone. transformers serve supports:
• voice cloning from a reference clip
• streaming, to hear the audio as it's generated
• instructions, to steer tone and style

And we tested it with VibeVoice, Higgs Audio V2 and Phonon. Any TTS model in transformers should work. If yours doesn't, open an issue and we'll add it!

Huge kudos to Eustache Le Bihan for the day-0 transformers integration, and Gradium team for open-sourcing their models. Phonon-31m is Apache 2.0 !

text:
Very excited to share that ContextCov has been accepted to #ICSE2027! 🎉

Coding agents can read AGENTS.md, but do they follow it? ContextCov turns natural-language repository instructions into executable checks for coding conventions, tooling restrictions, and architectural boundaries.

This one means a lot to me as a senior PhD student. I carried the project independently, from the initial idea through implementation, evaluation, and writing. Seeing it recognized is a meaningful milestone in my development as an independent researcher.

An earlier version also won Best Paper at the Agentic Software Engineering Workshop at ACM CAIS earlier this year! 

Only 119 of 2,375 submissions (~5%) received a direct accept. Having served on the shadow PC, I understand concerns about low-effort, AI-generated submissions, but I still find that figure strikingly low.

I am deeply grateful to my advisor and mentors for their guidance and support. Their encouragement has helped me grow as a researcher and take on projects with increasing independence.

In 1994, software was dead. People told me programming was for nerds and that I should become a doctor or a lawyer instead.

In 2004, software was dead. People told me that someone from India would take my job for $5/hour.

In 2014, software was dead. People told me that no-code was going to kill every job and doom my career.

In 2024, software was dead with Devin, Windsurf, Copilot, and OpenAI o1.

We kill software every 10 years, and yet the demand for good Software Engineers has never been higher.

it used to feel like the internet is moving and we're trying to catch up and read what's there and now it's the other way round that websites and tweets just sit there waiting to be slammed by ai agents

AI usefulness in every industry is capped by the speed with which generated proposals can be "noped" to get to the actual solution. In software, tests provide nearly instant nopes. For everything else there's nopekit. https://github.com/neuman/nopekit

We're making Shopify's mobile apps self-healing.

Agents watch production 24x7 for new crashes, reproduce them, write and verify a fix, then generate a short video explaining the root cause and the fix. Much faster to digest than the usual wall of text. 

An engineer then just reviews and ships it.
